label: Two-Dimensional Crystallography
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 50 through 66 and builds the symmetry theory of repeating planar patterns. We begin with two independent translations, refine the fundamental cell into a Dirichlet region, add rotations, reflections, and glides, and finish with the seventeen wallpaper groups that classify every periodic ornament in the plane.

label: Lattices and the Translation Group
notes: A plane lattice is the orbit of one point under two independent translations. Every lattice point is an integer combination of the basis vectors, so the translation subgroup is isomorphic to the integers crossed with the integers. The parallelogram spanned by the basis is a fundamental region whose area equals the determinant magnitude.

label: Fundamental Regions and Dirichlet Cells
notes: Any region that tiles the plane once per lattice point is a fundamental region, so the choice is far from unique. The canonical choice is the Dirichlet region, the Voronoi cell of nearest points. For a generic oblique basis it is a centrally symmetric hexagon; a rectangular basis collapses two sides and leaves a rectangle of equal area.

label: Motifs, Half-Turns, and Glides
notes: A wallpaper pattern is a motif carried by a lattice. Attaching an asymmetric motif under translations alone gives the group p1, while a glide reflection interleaves flipped copies. The defining relation is computational and exact: a glide performed twice is a pure translation, never the identity, which separates glides from ordinary mirrors.

label: Point Groups and Wallpaper Groups
notes: Each wallpaper group has a point group, the finite collection of rotations and reflections fixing a point after translations are quotiented out. Combining the allowed point groups with translations, and distinguishing genuine mirrors from glides, yields exactly seventeen plane crystallographic groups, from the trivial p1 to the fully symmetric p6m.

label: Six Patterns of Bricks
notes: The same two-to-one brick tiles the plane in several inequivalent ways. Offsetting rows, alternating orientation, or aligning them changes which local symmetries survive globally. Dashed lines mark mirrors, circles mark half-turns, squares mark quarter-turns, and half-arrows mark glides, giving six concrete wallpaper groups built from one shape.

label: The Crystallographic Restriction
notes: A discrete lattice cannot host every rotation order. Place two equal-period centers at minimum separation, rotate one about the other and back; for period five or beyond six this manufactures a closer same-period center, contradicting minimality. Only orders two, three, four, and six survive the nearest-center argument unscathed.

label: The Integer Trace Test
notes: The restriction has a clean algebraic proof. A rotation preserving a lattice acts as an integer matrix in a lattice basis, so its trace is an integer. A planar rotation of order n has trace two cosine of two pi over n, which is an integer only for n equal to one, two, three, four, or six. The geometry and the algebra agree.

label: Frieze Groups: The One-Dimensional Analogue
notes: Friezes are patterns periodic in a single direction, the strip analogue of wallpaper. Their translation subgroup is one copy of the integers, and the compatible point symmetries are half-turns, horizontal and vertical mirrors, and glides. These combine into exactly seven frieze groups, a small rehearsal for the richer seventeen-fold plane classification.

label: Regular Tessellations and Duality
notes: A regular tessellation brace p comma q places regular p-gons with q meeting at each vertex. The angle balance forces p minus two times q minus two to equal four, leaving only hexagons, squares, and triangles. Duality swaps faces and vertices, pairing the hexagonal and triangular tilings while the square tiling is self-dual.

label: Collinearity and Ordinary Lines
notes: Lattice fragments raise the Sylvester-Gallai question: can a finite noncollinear set avoid an ordinary line through exactly two points? Kelly's answer is no. Collinearity is tested by a three-by-three determinant, and the proof picks the point-line pair of least positive distance, deriving a contradiction if any third point lay on it.

label: Synthesis and Takeaways
notes: A planar lattice is a translation group plus the geometry of its cells, and the Dirichlet cell is its nearest-neighbor fundamental region. Adding rotations, mirrors, and glides yields seventeen wallpaper groups, constrained by the crystallographic restriction. Tessellations follow from one angle equation, and finite collinearity is decided by determinants.
